This cannon belonged to Gaspar Dias Fort which once stood near Miramar Circle. The construction of the fort began in 1598. The land where the fort was built, belonged to a Portuguese nobleman named Gaspar Dias. This fort, along with Reis Magos Fort on the other side of the river Mandovi, were built as defensive forts to protect the mouth of the river. From both the sides of the river, these two forts protected the area.

In 1835 there was a revolt within the fort premises. The revolt was put down and the fort was destroyed. Later, it was restored in 1842. In 1869, it was suggested that the fort could be used by convalescing soldiers and hence was turned into a sanatorium in 1878.

Eventually, the fort crumbled due to neglect and was razed to make way for changing times. Today, no signs of the fort can be found around Miramar Beach, except for the cannon at Miramar Circle. It is also said that some other cannons recovered from the fort have been kept at other locations.

The staff here is very kind and knowledgeable; they explain the stories and traditions connected to each part of the house in detail. Many Indian movies have been shot here because of its royal and authentic look.

A very special highlight is the small but sacred Ganpati Bappa idol, which holds great historical and spiritual importance for the family. Even after centuries, it is worshipped with deep devotion, showing how faith has been preserved through generations.

Overall, Casa Araujo Alvares is a must-visit heritage home for anyone who loves culture, history, and the timeless beauty of Goan tradition.

Absolutely worth visiting! The Portuguese house is a masterpiece, showcasing stunning architecture and various forms of exquisite art. The highlight of the visit was the incredible Lord Ganesha collection, featuring approximately 1,000 unique and beautifully crafted idols on display. Each piece reflects intricate craftsmanship and cultural significance, making it a truly captivating experience. A perfect blend of heritage, art, and devotion that shouldn’t be missed!

We love grand architecture anywhere in the world, and in Goa, Casa Araujo Alvares is a gem! 💎🏰 A 17th-century mansion filled with antiques, chandeliers, and just the right amount of old-money drama. If these walls could talk, they’d probably gossip. ☕👀

But the highlight? The wonderfully old-school, slightly dramatic history tour! 🎤💃🏽 You’ll be led from room to room while a deep, mysterious voice tells the story of Goa’s colonial past—accompanied by the odd life-sized mannequin that definitely look like they might move when you blink. 👀🤖

It’s a popular attraction with locals, and it’s easy to see why—because who doesn’t love a bit of time travel, aristocratic flair, and the occasional wait😳

A visit to ASI-protected sites is truly a must for history lovers, architecture enthusiasts, and anyone who wants to see Goa’s cultural side.

Sonshe Waterfalls is a hidden gem in Goa, offering a pristine natural experience away from the usual tourist crowds. My visit here was absolutely magical.

Highlights:

Natural Beauty: The waterfall is nestled amidst dense forests and cascades down beautifully, creating a serene and picturesque environment. The lush greenery and the sound of rushing water make it a perfect retreat for nature enthusiasts.
Tranquil Atmosphere: Unlike some of the more popular waterfalls, Sonshe Waterfalls offers a peaceful and secluded atmosphere. It’s an ideal spot for relaxation and unwinding.
Refreshing Experience: The clear, cool water is perfect for a refreshing dip. Swimming in the natural pool at the base of the waterfall was a highlight of my visit.
Hiking Opportunity: The trek to the waterfall is an adventure in itself. The trail is surrounded by rich flora and fauna, making the hike enjoyable and rewarding.
Improvements:

Accessibility: The trail leading to the waterfall can be challenging, especially during the monsoon season. Better signage and maintenance of the path would make it more accessible for all visitors.
Facilities: There are minimal facilities available at the site. Adding basic amenities such as restrooms and seating areas would be beneficial for visitors.
Overall, Sonshe Waterfalls is a must-visit for anyone seeking a serene and natural escape in Goa. Whether you’re an adventurer, a nature lover, or simply looking to relax, this place has something special to offer.

Brahma Waterfall is such a hidden gem! The trek is super easy—just around 10 minutes—and totally worth it. Along the way, you actually come across three stunning waterfalls, each more beautiful than the last.

Brahma Karmali Waterfalls (also spelled Bramha Karmali or Brahmakarmali) is a set of charming mini waterfalls tucked away in the Mhadei Wildlife Sanctuary near Naneli/Valpoi in North Goa. Here's a detailed guide:

---

🌿 What Makes It Special

Easily accessible: Just a ~1 km gentle trek from the parking spot brings you to the first cascade—a broad, tranquil stream ideal for picnics and family swims  .

Multiple small falls: If you explore further along converging streams, you’ll find 2–3 more serene cascades, perfect for wading  .

Ideal for all: No steep cliffs or deep plunge pools—just clean flowing water and lush surroundings  .

---

🕒 Entry & Essentials

Entry Fee: ₹100 per adult (Goa Forest Department)  .

Timing: Open from roughly 6 AM to 6 PM daily  .

Best time to visit: During and just after the monsoon (July–September), when the falls are fullest  .

Facilities: None—carry drinking water, snacks and wear comfortable shoes  .

---

🚶 Getting There

By car or bike: Drive towards Naneli/Valpoi via Ponda—follow signs for Bramha Karmali‑Shelphem Rd, H5M6+24G location  .

By bus + walking: Take a Ponda–Naneli bus, then walk ~500 m to the trailhead  .

Guided trek: Especially popular in monsoon—local guides can help you navigate forest paths  .

---

🧭 Trek & Trail Experience

Trail difficulty: Easy to moderate, with occasional water crossings; takes about 30–45 minutes one way  .

Family-friendly: Schools and trekking groups often visit—the 2019 Valpoi trek by students was well organized and safe  .

Nature & wildlife: You walk through dense Western Ghats forests where you may hear birds and monkeys; terrain is lush and enchanting during rains  .

---

🏞️ Insider Tips

Monsoon magic: The falls are at their most dramatic during/after heavy rains; the surrounding forest feels mystical  .

Carry your own gear: There are no shops or restrooms—come prepared  .

Visit early: For quieter experience and softer light for photos.

Respect nature: Keep the trails clean, carry waste back—it's a pristine sanctuary.

---

✅ Is It Worth Visiting?

Absolutely—especially if you're looking for a short, gentle trek in Goa’s lush interior with beautiful and safe mini waterfalls ideal for families or peaceful solo explorers. It’s not a showstopping cascade like Dudhsagar or Harvalem, but its charm lies in its serenity, ease, and natural beauty  .

---

🔄 Nearby Attractions to Explore

Harvalem (Arvalem) Falls – bigger and more touristy.

Other nearby hidden gems: Karmalya, Mainapi, Tambdi Surla, all within ~30–70 km radius
---

Caranzol Talyar Waterfall is a hidden gem tucked away in the lush forests of the Talyar region. As a nature enthusiast and avid hiker, I was absolutely blown away by the beauty of this waterfall and the surrounding scenery.

Baga Beach is one of the most famous and lively beaches in North Goa, and after my visit, I can confidently say it’s a must-visit destination for anyone coming to Goa.

We visited as a group around 8 PM to experience the vibrant Goa nightlife, and the atmosphere was truly electric. The entire beach was beautifully lit and decorated by the stall owners, creating a mesmerizing view with the sound of the waves adding to the magic. The tides were strong and rhythmic, perfectly complementing the lively vibe around.

Almost every food stall or shack had its own DJ night setup, where people were dancing freely and enjoying the music under the open sky. Near the shore, several stalls had arranged cozy seating areas with creative props for clicking pictures — making it a perfect spot for both fun and relaxation.

We chose a stall offering a candlelight dinner setup with soothing background music and waves crashing just a few steps away. The ambience was simply wonderful — romantic, peaceful, and refreshing at the same time.

The food prices were slightly on the higher side, but the experience and ambience made it completely worth it. If you want to feel the true Goan nightlife vibe with music, sea breeze, and great food, Baga Beach is the perfect place to be.

All major water sports like jet ski rides, banana boating, parasailing, and speed boating are available here, and the rates are quite standardized and well controlled by local authorities. Trained lifeguards are always on duty, which adds to the feeling of safety.

There are plenty of food and drink options — from beach shacks serving Goan seafood to juice stalls and cafés nearby. The beach also has areas marked for bathing, although the state-provided bathing section is not very clean and can be better maintained.

Parking is available near the main entrance, and reaching the beach is easy from any part of North Goa. It gets crowded during weekends and evenings, but that’s part of its charm.

Overall, a fun place to spend half a day — ideal for families, couples, and adventure lovers alike! 🌴🌊

Querim Beach (Keri Beach): A Serene Escape in North Goa

Querim Beach, also known as Keri Beach, is a tranquil haven located at the northernmost tip of Goa. Far from the bustling crowds of more commercialized beaches, Querim offers a peaceful retreat amidst natural beauty. ￼

Natural Beauty and Tranquility

Stretching over 2 kilometers, Querim Beach boasts pristine white sands bordered by lush greenery and rocky outcrops. The beach is lined with pine and palm trees, providing shade and enhancing its serene ambiance. The calm and clear waters, coupled with the gentle sea breeze, create an ideal setting for relaxation and solitude.  ￼ ￼

Activities and Attractions

While Querim Beach is less commercialized, it offers several activities for visitors:
•	Water Sports: Adventurous souls can indulge in activities like paragliding, jet skiing, banana boat rides, and kayaking.  ￼
•	Dolphin Spotting: The beach is known for its abundant dolphin population, especially active during early mornings.  ￼
•	Exploration: Visitors can explore the nearby Querim Caves, accessible during low tide, and the historic Tiracol Fort, which offers panoramic views of the Arabian Sea and has been converted into a heritage hotel.  ￼

Culinary Delights

Querim Beach features several beach shacks and eateries serving authentic Goan cuisine. Notable spots include ‘Rice Bowl’ for Asian delicacies, ‘Suzie’s’ offering fusion dishes and cocktails, and ‘This Is It’ specializing in traditional Goan fare.  ￼

Accommodation Options

Accommodation near Querim Beach ranges from budget-friendly guesthouses to luxury resorts. Options include Fort Tiracol Heritage Hotel, Hotel Hill Rock Goa, Lotus Sutra Resort, and Gods Gift Guesthouse, catering to various preferences and budgets.  ￼ ￼

Best Time to Visit

The ideal time to visit Querim Beach is between October and March, when the weather is pleasant, and the sea is calm. It’s advisable to avoid the monsoon season, as the beach can be unsafe due to strong currents and steep inclines.  ￼

Conclusion

Querim Beach stands out as a serene and less crowded destination in Goa, offering natural beauty, cultural attractions, and a range of activities. It’s an ideal spot for those seeking tranquility away from the typical tourist trails.

A 4-Star Coastal Retreat with Room for Improvement

Varca Beach offers visitors a serene escape with its pristine surroundings and inviting atmosphere. Whether you’re planning a relaxing day under the sun or a peaceful evening by the water, Varca Beach stands out for its natural beauty and well-maintained environment.

Highlights of Varca Beach
•	Immaculate Cleanliness:
The beach is remarkably clean with well-preserved sands and crystal-clear water. The efforts to maintain this cleanliness are evident, making it an ideal spot for families and individuals who appreciate a pristine coastal environment.

•	Well-Maintained Ambiance:
The overall upkeep of Varca Beach is commendable. From its tidy surroundings to the organized layout, every detail contributes to a delightful experience. The atmosphere here is relaxed and inviting—perfect for unwinding or enjoying leisurely strolls along the shore.

•	Amazing Natural Atmosphere:
The beach offers a tranquil ambiance that complements its scenic beauty. The combination of clean water, soft sands, and the soothing sounds of the ocean creates an idyllic environment that is hard to match.

Areas for Improvement
•	Lighting Post Sunset:
One noticeable drawback is the inadequate lighting after sunset. This can pose difficulties, especially for elderly visitors, who may find it challenging to navigate the area or locate exits safely once the sun goes down.

•	Safety Measures and Lifeguards:
Another area where Varca Beach could improve is safety. Currently, there are no lifeguards or additional safety measures in place to handle any untoward incidents. For families and solo travelers alike, this is an important factor to consider when planning a visit.

Overall Experience

Varca Beach earns a solid 4-star rating for its cleanliness, well-maintained facilities, and inviting natural ambiance. It is a great destination for those looking to enjoy a quiet, scenic day by the sea. However, potential visitors should be mindful of the limited lighting after sunset and the absence of dedicated safety personnel.

If you’re planning a visit, it might be best to schedule your time during daylight hours to fully appreciate the beauty and serenity Varca Beach offers. With a few improvements in safety and evening infrastructure, this coastal gem could easily become a top-tier destination for beach lovers.

🚤 Coco Beach: North Goa's Dolphin Spotting and River Cruise Hub! 🌴
RATING: ⭐⭐⭐⭐ (4/5 – Excellent for Activity, Not for Swimming)

Coco Beach, situated in the Nerul area near Reis Magos, occupies a unique geographical position: it's nestled right at the mouth of the Mandovi River where it meets the Arabian Sea. It is a vital artery for Goan water tourism, serving primarily as the main jetty and departure point for boat trips and dolphin spotting, rather than a traditional sunbathing beach.

The Signature Coco Beach Experience
The Hub of Adventure: Coco Beach's raison d'être is activity. It is the most popular and organized spot in North Goa to hire a boat for dolphin watching tours (best done early morning) and scenic river cruises that navigate the Mandovi and Chapora estuaries.

Unique Scenery: Due to its proximity to the river, the sand here is darker and more silty than the pure golden sands of Calangute or Sinquerim. This isn't the place for swimming or laying out a towel, but it offers a beautiful, unique view across the water to the headlands of Panjim and Dona Paula.

The Reis Magos Context: The beach lies directly below the Reis Magos Fort, offering a historical backdrop. The view from the water looking back at the dense, coconut palm groves that line the shore is classic Goan scenery.

Vibe and Function
The atmosphere is perpetually bustling and commercial, characterized by boat operators, ticket sellers, and travelers getting ready for their excursions. It is highly functional and convenient. It lacks the laid-back lounging feel of the Arabian Sea beaches but buzzes with the excitement of impending adventure.

📸 Pro-Tips for Visitors
Go Early for Dolphins: If dolphin spotting is your goal, you must arrive before 9 AM. The boats leave early, and the dolphins are most active in the quiet morning hours.

Manage Expectations: Treat Coco Beach as a maritime transit point, not a relaxing beach. If you want pristine sand and calm swimming, head just down the road to Candolim or Sinquerim.

Negotiate Prices: While the boat operators are generally regulated, it's wise to confirm the duration and inclusions of your trip before boarding.

Photography: The best photo opportunities are from the boat, capturing the lush river banks and the distant views of Panjim and the coastline.

Conclusion: Coco Beach is an essential destination for any traveler wanting to get out onto the water in North Goa. While you won't spend the day sunbathing here, it serves as the perfect, convenient gateway to river cruises, dolphin spotting, and exploring the beautiful Mandovi estuary.

🤫 Nuem Beach: South Goa's Whisper and Uncharted Sanctuary! 🧭
RATING: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (5/5 – Perfect for Unspoiled Nature and Absolute Seclusion)

Nuem Beach is a name known only to the most dedicated local residents and seasoned explorers. It is not on the main tourist map; rather, it is one of the many ultra-secluded, tiny coves and pristine stretches tucked deep into South Goa, typically south of the Sal River estuary, that lack major commercial development. If you are seeking a truly untouched, raw, and silent coastal experience—a place to meditate, read, or enjoy nature completely alone—this is the destination for the adventurous soul.

The Signature Nuem Experience
Purity and Isolation: The primary draw of Nuem (or whichever secluded cove it refers to) is the complete absence of commercial activity. There are no shacks, no vendors, and almost zero tourist crowds. This results in sand that is cleaner and a natural environment that is entirely undisturbed.

Raw Natural Beauty: The beach is often backed by dense coastal vegetation and rugged, rocky headlands. This juxtaposition of untouched greenery and the blue ocean creates a dramatically picturesque landscape that feels prehistoric and remote.

Safety and Self-Sufficiency: The water in these secluded coves is generally calm and clean, but the lack of official lifeguard supervision means swimming requires extra caution. This beach demands that you be entirely self-sufficient.

Atmosphere and Accessibility
The atmosphere is one of profound, restorative peace. Life here is slow and quiet. You might only share the sand with a few local fishermen mending their nets or a handful of residents enjoying a quiet moment.

Accessibility Note: Reaching this type of remote beach often involves navigating small, unmarked, and sometimes steep dirt tracks. It is usually best accessed by scooter or on foot, and finding the final descent can be part of the adventure itself.

📸 Pro-Tips for Visitors
Pack Everything In/Out: Since there are no facilities, you must bring all your water, snacks, and shade (if needed). More importantly, you must take all trash back out with you to preserve the pristine nature of the cove.

Swimming Caution: Only swim in safe, calm conditions and never swim alone, as there are no emergency services nearby.

Photography: The best time for photography is early morning, when the light is soft, and the shadows from the surrounding hills are dramatic, highlighting the untouched nature of the shore.

Respect Local Life: If you encounter local fishermen, maintain distance and respect their work, as their primary livelihood depends on this quiet stretch of coast.

Conclusion: If the noise and crowds of the major tourist beaches are exactly what you are trying to escape, Nuem Beach represents the highest level of South Goan seclusion. It’s an essential experience for those seeking deep solitude and raw, unspoiled coastal beauty.

**Bogmalo Beach, Dabolim, Goa**

Bogmalo Beach, located just a few kilometers from Dabolim Airport in Goa, is a serene and lesser-known gem compared to the bustling beaches of Baga or Calangute. This small, crescent-shaped beach offers a peaceful retreat with soft golden sands, clear waters, and a relaxed vibe, making it perfect for those seeking tranquility.

### **Highlights:**
✔ **Less Crowded** – Unlike popular North Goa beaches, Bogmalo remains relatively untouched by mass tourism, offering a more laid-back experience.
✔ **Clean & Scenic** – The beach is well-maintained, with clean shores and gentle waves, ideal for swimming and sunbathing.
✔ **Dining Options** – A few beach shacks and restaurants serve delicious Goan seafood, refreshing drinks, and international cuisine at reasonable prices.
✔ **Water Sports** – While not as commercialized as other beaches, Bogmalo offers activities like jet skiing and parasailing for adventure seekers.
✔ **Proximity to Airport** – Its location near Dabolim Airport (just 4 km away) makes it a convenient stop for travelers arriving or departing Goa.

### **Drawbacks:**
❌ **Limited Nightlife** – If you're looking for parties and vibrant nightlife, Bogmalo may feel too quiet.
❌ **Small Size** – The beach is compact, so it can get slightly crowded during peak season.

### Bogmalo Beach is an excellent choice for couples, families, and solo travelers who prefer a calm, scenic beach away from the crowds. While it lacks the wild energy of North Goa, its natural beauty and relaxed atmosphere make it a hidden paradise worth visiting.

The Arvalem Caves are popularly known as ''Pandava Caves''. According to the history, the five Pandavas of the epic Mahabharata sought refuge in these caves during their exile. The Arvalem Caves are very much patterned in the Buddhist cave style. The architecture of the caves is simple yet appealing. The walls are plain with no paintings on them. The rock structure has been cut into laterite stone, with the sanctuary at the northern end and the vihara at the southern end. The mysterious look of the caves has been attracting the tourists over long years. The presence of the famous Rudreshwar temple and a waterfall in its vicinity, makes this place a must visit in Goa.

There are five compartments in the cave complex and the middle compartment enshrines the 'linga' held in great reverence by devotees. The shafts of the four crafted lingas are very similar to those that can be found in Elephanta, Ajanta and Ellora caves in Maharashtra. The Shivalinga in the second cave is engraved with an inscription written in Sanskrit and Brahmi characters of the 7th century. The Shivalinga and the inscription are assigned to the period of the Bhoja King Kapalivarman. The complex consists of two major caves and a residential chamber.

Nearby tourist spots are Arvalem Water Falls (1.3 kms) and St. John of The Cross, Sanquelim(2.2 kms).

The Church of St. Augustine in Old Goa is one of the most hauntingly beautiful ruins in India—a silent witness to centuries of faith, grandeur, and eventual decades

🏛️ Church of St. Augustine – Goa’s Towering Memory

🕰️ History & Legacy
- Built between 1597 and 1602 by Augustinian friars, the church was once among the largest in Goa and part of a vast religious complex.
- It was dedicated to Our Lady of Grace and included a convent, eight chapels, and four altars.
- After the Augustinians were expelled in 1835, the church was abandoned. The main vault collapsed in 1846, and by 1938, most of the structure had crumbled.

🗼 The Tower That Remains
- Today, the most iconic remnant is the 46-meter-high bell tower, built of laterite stone. It’s the only surviving part of the original four towers.
- The bell that once hung here now resides in the Church of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception in Panaji.

🧭 Visitor Experience
- Located on Monte Santo (Holy Hill) in Old Goa, the site offers a quiet, reflective atmosphere.
- It’s part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site cluster and is often featured in films and photography for its dramatic ruins.
- Archaeological excavations here even uncovered relics believed to belong to Queen Ketevan of Georgia, adding an international layer

Basilica of Bom Jesus, Roman Catholic church in the abandoned city of Old Goa, Goa state, India. Built between 1594 and 1605, it is regarded as an outstanding example of Renaissance Baroque and Portuguese colonial architecture. The basilica is also known for housing the remains of the missionary St. Francis Xavier, who was based in Goa in 1541–49.

Old Goa was the original capital of the former Portuguese colony of Goa and once rivaled Lisbon in size and splendor. It was the first Jesuit colony in the Indian subcontinent and in 1565 could boast a population of 200,000. However, malaria and cholera epidemics ravaged the city in the seventeenth century and it was then largely abandoned.

Construction of the huge Basilica of Bom Jesus (“Good Jesus”) began in 1594, and it was consecrated in 1605. It attained status as a basilica in 1946. Cruciform in plan, its facade combines Ionic, Doric, Corinthian, and composite styles. Three elegant entrances are surmounted by three large rectangular windows, then three smaller circular windows, culminating in a richly carved central gable.

The chapel and tomb of St. Francis Xavier—a student and companion of St. Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits—lie on the south side of the transept. The ornate tomb was a gift from Grand Duke Cosimo III of Tuscany. Carved by Giovanni Battista Foggini, it was begun in 1689 and was erected in 1698. The silver-covered casket containing St. Francis’s remains is a magnificent hybrid of Italian and Indian art; a painstaking restoration was completed in 2021. When the saint’s body was transferred here a year after his death it was said to be “as fresh as the day it was buried.” St. Francis is credited with miraculous healing powers. His feast day, December 3, is observed every year, and his body is displayed to the faithful and carried in procession every ten years, attracting pilgrims from far and wide.

The Basilica of Bom Jesus is among the group of “Churches and Convents of Goa” listed as a World Heritage site in 1986. In addition to being open to tourists, the basilica hosts mass daily.

No tour in Old Goa is complete without visiting the Church of St Francis of Assisi that is joined by an old palace of the Archbishop to another popular church in the state, Se Cathedral. Close to the Church of St Francis of Assisi, a convent was built which was converted into an Archaeological Museum of History in 1964. The museum is one of the prime attractions of this popular church in Goa.

History of Church of St. Francis of Assisi

The history of Church of St. Francis of Assisi states that it was first built in 1521 by the Fransican monks. When this structure started to decay, a new church started to build in 1665 which retained the portal of the old structure done in Portuguese–Manueline style.

Architecture of Church of St. Francis of Assisi

The architecture of the Church of St. Francis of Assisi is an interesting mix of Tuscan and Portuguese-Manueline style. The façade of the church is built in the Tuscan style of architecture with the portal being Manueline since it is retained from the older structure. The façade of the church is distinctive as it is flanked by octagonal towers and a small niche housing the statue of Our Lady of Miracles brought from Jaffna in Sri Lanka.

Immerse in Art and Culture at Sunaparanta

Nestled in the serene Altinho hills of Panjim, the Sunaparanta, Goa Centre for the Arts, is a vibrant cultural hub that offers a delightful blend of traditional Goan charm and contemporary art. Founded in 2009 by the visionary Dattaraj V. Salgaocar, this non-profit center aims to preserve Goa's artistic legacy while fostering modern creative expressions.

The term "Sunaparanta" is rooted in Buddhist tradition, combining "Suna" (a place) and "Aparanta" (the region of fierce people), aptly reflecting the center's bold and dynamic approach to art. Housed in a beautifully restored Portuguese bungalow, the center boasts terracotta roofs, sweeping staircases, and a central courtyard that enhances its rustic yet grand aesthetic.

Art lovers can immerse themselves in a variety of exhibitions featuring both local and international artists. The center is well-known for its eclectic programming, including the annual Sensorium Festival, which explores the intersection of various art forms such as photography, literature, and cinema. Additionally, the Shanghvi Salons offer intellectually stimulating discussions with renowned personalities from the creative world.

Sunaparanta also hosts workshops, film screenings, and children's programs, making it a lively space for artistic engagement. Notable programs include "Film for Thought," which screens critically acclaimed films, and "In Stages," a theatre workshop for teenagers.

The open-air Café Al Fresco is a must-visit, serving delectable dishes in a charming setting. It’s the perfect spot to enjoy a leisurely meal while soaking in the artistic ambiance.

Open from Monday to Saturday, 10 AM to 6:30 PM, Sunaparanta is a cultural gem in Goa that transcends the typical beach-centric allure of the state. Entrance is free, though certain events may require prior registration.

Abbé Faria (Portuguese: Abade Faria), or Abbé (Abbot) José Custódio de Faria (31 May 1756 – 20 September 1819), was a Luso-Goan Catholic monk who was one of the pioneers of the scientific study of hypnotism, following on from the work of Franz Mesmer. Unlike Mesmer, who claimed that hypnosis was mediated by "animal magnetism", Faria understood that it worked purely by the power of suggestion. In the early 19th century, Abbé Faria introduced oriental hypnosis to Paris.

He was one of the first to depart from the theory of the "magnetic fluid", to place in relief the importance of suggestion, and to demonstrate the existence of "autosuggestion"; he also established that what he termed nervous sleep belongs to the natural order. From his earliest magnetizing séances, in 1814, he boldly developed his doctrine. Nothing comes from the magnetizer; everything comes from the subject and takes place in his imagination generated from within the mind. Magnetism is only a form of sleep. Although of the moral order, the magnetic action is often aided by physical, or rather by physiological, means–fixedness of look and cerebral fatigue.

Faria changed the terminology of mesmerism. Previously, the focus was on the "concentration" of the subject. In Faria's terminology the operator became "the concentrator" and somnambulism was viewed as a lucid sleep. The method of hypnosis used by Faria is command, following expectancy. The theory of Abbé Faria is now known as Fariism.

Later, Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault (1864–1904), the founder of the Nancy School, and Émile Coué (1857–1926), father of applied conditioning, developed the theory of suggestion and autosuggestion and began using them as therapeutic tools. Johannes Schultz developed these theories as Autogenic training.

⚓ Nauxim Beach: Zuari Bay's Secret Balcony and Tranquil Anchor! 🤫
RATING: ⭐⭐⭐⭐ (4/5 – Uncommercialized Peace and Unique Harbor Views)

Nauxim Beach is one of Goa's best-kept secrets, tucked away on the western side of the Tiswadi peninsula, facing the vast Zuari Bay instead of the open Arabian Sea. This difference in location fundamentally changes the experience. It is a place of profound tranquility, primarily used by local fishermen and residents, offering a panoramic view that is both natural and industrial, making it truly unique.

The Signature Nauxim Experience
Bay-Side Tranquility: Since Nauxim is sheltered deep within the bay, the water is exceptionally calm and placid. The environment is lush, backed by rolling hills and thick coconut groves, providing a beautiful, uncommercialized backdrop far removed from the typical North Goa hustle.

Unique Dual View: Nauxim provides a distinctive vista across the wide expanse of the Zuari River estuary. From the shore, you can clearly see the active Mormugao Harbour and often catch sight of large cargo ships and the Dabolim Airport runway in the distance. This unique blend of untouched nature in the foreground and busy industry/maritime traffic in the background is fascinating.

A Local and Natural Vibe: This is not a tourist beach. You won't find large shacks or loud music. Instead, you'll encounter local fishing canoes (dongi), fishermen mending their nets, and the occasional jogger. It’s an ideal spot for quiet contemplation and long, peaceful walks.

Safe for Paddling: Due to the extremely calm water, it is safe for children to wade and paddle, though swimming should be approached with caution due to the bay water's proximity to river mouths and port activities.

Atmosphere and Accessibility
Nauxim's atmosphere is rustic and authentic. There is minimal tourist infrastructure, emphasizing its secluded nature. Access is via a small, winding road off the main route, ensuring that only those truly seeking peace find their way here.

📸 Pro-Tips for Visitors
Bring Your Own: As commercial activity is minimal, it is advisable to bring your own water, snacks, and gear. Don't rely on finding a full-service beach shack here.

Photography Focus: The best time for photos is at sunset, as the sun drops behind the distant headlands and the lights of the Mormugao Port and harbor ships begin to twinkle across the bay, creating a beautiful contrast.

Nature Observation: The calm waters and surrounding mangroves make it a good spot for quiet bird watching in the early morning.

Perfect for Picnics: Due to its serenity and ample shade from the trees, Nauxim is perfect for a peaceful picnic far from the crowds.

Conclusion: Nauxim Beach offers a rare glimpse of Goa's untouched, river-mouth beauty. It’s the perfect, secluded escape for those seeking quiet, natural scenery and a fascinating, panoramic view of the state's maritime core.

Imagine a small trading town in the Balkan region having an outpost on the west coast of India nearly 500 years ago.

Not many people who visit Goa know that in the north, in the village of Gandaulim is the St. Blaise Church which is all that remains of Goa’s Croatian connection.

If you're travelling from Ponda, I would recommend you to take the Marcel route. Its closer.

Visitors from Croatia came to Gandaulim, about 4km from Old Goa, sometime in the 16th century

They may have not dwelled there for long, but the restored Church of Sao Braz that they built

Since 1999, the village has been getting visitors, with Croats developing an emotional attachment to the place

It was quite by chance that Croatian Indologist Zdravka Matišic discovered a reference to her country’s Goa links while studying Sanskrit in India. Matišic carried out further research in the state’s archives. The grand sight of the Church of Sao Braz — a much smaller version of Sveti Vlaho Church in Dubrovnik, Croatia — silhouetted against a blue sky is said to have filled her with joy. However, she was disappointed to find the riverside entrance to the church, styled like the arch on Dubrovnik harbour, in ruins. The PWD knocked it down to allow vehicles to reach the ferry point at the canal two decades ago.

On April 1, 1999, the first official delegation from Croatia arrived in Gandaulim to explore the Goa-Croatia links of yore. The 15-member parliamentary delegation was accompanied by Croatian ambassador to India Zoran Andric.

Historians think the Portuguese may have brought the Croatians to build ships — their expertise in this field was respected — or they may have arrived in the village of Gandaulim, then a teeming suburb of Old Goa, as merchants.

Portuguese writer Gomes Catao in his book refers to a population of 12,000 during its glory days. Women from the affluent strata of society here were transported in palanquins by slaves to the Sao Braz church, Gomes writes.

Since 1999, the village has been getting visitors, with the Croats developing an emotional attachment to the place. “Every time a Croatian ship comes to the Mormugao harbour, the sailors come to visit our church,” a villager, Braz Silveira, says. A Croatian pediatrician, Dr Marija Radonic, who came more than a decade ago, went back and collected donations for the church, he adds. “I visited her home two years ago, and she has pictures of our church before and after the restoration,” he says.

Tea Batinic, an art gallery owner in Dubrovnik, donated his paintings to the church after a visit. These were auctioned to fund church repairs.

Last year, a Croatian team visited the village to film a documentary. “We are waiting to see the documentary that records the historical landmarks in our village,” says a resident, Esperance Silveira e Vaz. The rapport between villagers and Croatians has grown over the years. “The relationship with the people of Dubrovnik is very close to my heart, especially after I stayed with them for three days,” Braz Silveira says.
This Church is a replica of the one in Dubrovnik. Originally the St. Blaise Church, Sao Bras was a small Chapel built in 1541 by Croatian sailors and traders settled in this village.

Margao, often called the commercial capital of Goa, is the capital of the southern taluka of Salcette and also of the South Goa district. Because of its location, it serves as a service and transport hub to the areas of south Goa.It is a typically crowded Goan town, with chaotic, noisy traffic and quite a few architectural reminders of its Portuguese past. Margao is Goa’s second largest town and a bustling commercial centre.Surrounded by fertile farmland, the town of Margao was once a major religious centre, with dozens of wealthy temples and dharmshalas (dormitories). In fact the name Margao is thought to be the Portuguese corruption of the word Mathgram (from Math – a Hindu religious centre that used to exist there). However most of these were destroyed when the Portuguese absorbed the area into their Novas Conquistas during the 17th century.Margao has an old-worldly charm about it because of its Portuguese churches, and some magnificent specimens of old Portuguese houses complete with shady balcaos (porches) and oyster-shell windows in its Borda area.The Largo de Igreja, or the Church of the Holy Spirit as it is also known, dominates the entrance to the city, just north of the Municipal Garden square. The church area is surrounded by beautiful old residential houses still in pristine condition. The church was built by the Portuguese in 1675 and is one of the finest examples of late-Baroque architecture in Goa, boasting a pristine white façade and an interior dripping with gilt crystal and stucco.Just within walking distance of the Church, is the famous “House of Seven Gables” or “Sat Burzam Ghor”. This magnificent mansion was commissioned in 1790 by Sebastino da Silva, emissary and private secretary of the Portuguese Viceroy. Although only three of the seven gables remain today, they are enough to give the visitor an idea of the size of the original edifice.The town has an excellent market area stretching from the south edge of the main square to within a stone’s throw of the old railway station. The Bazaar centres on a labyrinthine covered area that’s a rich source of authentic souvenirs and a good place to browse for some bargain shopping.In the centre of the town is the Municipal Garden (known as Praça Jorge Barreto), around which most restaurants and office buildings are located. The colonial style red washed Municipal building built in 1905 and the Library lie on the park’s south side. From this main square, bylanes lead to the bazaar and the area that used to be the fish market.

Margao’s fish market was earlier located opposite the Municipal building and was a spectacular sight, with the fisherwomen from coastal areas of South Goa hawking their wares at the top of their voices, dressed in superbly coloured cotton sarees. The market has since been shifted to a complex located at the entrance of the city.The road from the Largo de Igreja splits into two at the entrance to Margao, one going into the proper city and the other winding up towards another Margao landmark. This road called Calçada de Nossa Senhora de Piedade leads up to Monte Hill. There is a small chapel at the top of the hill which remains locked most of the time. But it is worth coming up here for a spectacular view of the Salcette countryside in general and Margao in particular.The famous Colva beach is just 6 kilometers away from Margao, so most travelers coming to this area of Goa, tend to spend their time in the beach area, rather than enjoy the charms of Margao town itself.There are some interesting places around Margao. About 3 Km. from the small village of Raia, which is on the road from Margao to the Borim Bridge, is the Rachol Seminary and Church. Margao is also the last stop for a number of trains coming to Goa especially from Mumbai.

Little Beach in Goa is a hidden gem that offers a truly magical experience, whether you visit in the early morning or during sunset. Having had the pleasure of experiencing both times of day, I can confidently say that this beach is a must-visit.

The gentle sound of the waves, the soft morning light, and the peaceful atmosphere create a perfect setting for relaxation and reflection. The beach is less crowded at this time, allowing you to fully immerse yourself in the natural beauty of the surroundings. The golden hues of the sunrise cast a warm glow over the sand and water, making it a picturesque start to the day.

During sunset, Little Beach transforms into a vibrant and captivating scene. The sky is painted with stunning shades of orange, pink, and purple, creating a breathtaking backdrop as the sun dips below the horizon. The beach comes alive with the energy of both locals and tourists, all gathered to witness the mesmerizing sunset. It's a wonderful time to take a leisurely stroll along the shore, capture stunning photographs, or simply relax and enjoy the view.

In conclusion, Little Beach is a must-recommended place in Goa. Whether you seek peace and solitude in the early morning or the vibrant beauty of a sunset, this beach offers an unforgettable experience. Don't miss the opportunity to visit this incredible destination.

Our Lady of Assumption Church in Sarzora, Goa is a beautiful and peaceful place of worship. The church stands tall and majestic, with its white façade and intricate architectural details. The surrounding area is well-maintained and gives a serene and calming atmosphere.

The interior of the church is equally stunning, with its carved wooden ceiling and vibrant stained glass windows depicting religious scenes and figures. The altar is the centerpiece, adorned with delicate flowers and candles, creating a sense of reverence and devotion.

The church regularly holds mass and other religious services, which are attended by the local community and tourists alike. The priests and staff are warm and welcoming, making everyone feel at home. The service is conducted with utmost reverence and devotion, creating a spiritual atmosphere that touches the heart.

The church also hosts various festivals and events throughout the year. The Feast of Our Lady of Assumption, celebrated on August 15th, is a major highlight. The church is beautifully decorated, and a procession takes place where the statue of Our Lady is carried through the streets, accompanied by music and hymns. It is a joyous and vibrant celebration that brings people together in faith and community.

Visiting Our Lady of Assumption Church is not only a religious experience but also an opportunity to appreciate the rich cultural heritage of Goa. The church is a historical landmark, dating back to the Portuguese colonial era. It serves as a reminder of the deep-rooted Christian faith in the region.

The church is easily accessible, and parking facilities are available nearby. The peaceful surroundings and beautiful scenery make it a perfect place for reflection and prayer. If you are visiting Goa, do not miss the chance to visit Our Lady of Assumption Church in Sarzora.

In conclusion, Our Lady of Assumption Church in Sarzora, Goa is a must-visit for anyone seeking a place of tranquility, spirituality, and cultural significance. The stunning architecture, warm hospitality, and spiritual atmosphere make it a true gem in the region.

St. Thomas Church, Cansaulim, Goa is called ‘Sao Tome Igreja em Cansaulim, Goa’ in Portuguese. It was established in the mid of 16th century by the Jesuits missionary as a Chapel. Around 1588 AD a grand Church was built which is dedicated to St. Thomas. This is an ancient Church built in Portuguese architectural style which has many remarkable features with triple storeyed quite imposing faced.

Central part of the faced is erected on four ribbed pillars and the centre of the Church's top is adorned with the Holy cross and below a statue covered with glass, below an arched window then entrance at the ground.

Faced bears the triangular spires at the capital of the pillars as either side of the Holy Cross these pillars are extended to three stages and the central pillars up to four stages. It has cornice and the basalt stones surface is covered with lime plaster. The interior is very attractive and the altar is marvelous. There are many statues and Chandeliers suspended to the ceiling.

Our Lady of the Poor Church is located in Nuvem Village. It is also known as Igreja Mae dos Pobres (Mother of the Poor Church) or The Holy Family Church. The main altar of the church is actually dedicated to Jesus, Mary and Joseph in 1695. It was affiliated to the parish of the Holy Spirit Church, Margao. Nuvem became a separate parish in 1903.

The Church was built in Neo-Roman-Mannerist architecture. It is the only heritage structure in the village of Nuvem has been plunged into a bitter row over an alleged proposal for its demolition for a bigger church.

The Mother of the Poor Church feast is celebrated by the villagers on the first Sunday of November. The statue of Mae Dos Pobres being taken in a procession at Jesus and Mary Church on the occasion of the feast which was celebrated with pomp and gaiety.

The feast of Mae dos Pobres brings people from the neighbouring villages to Nuvem to pray for grace and favours from Mother Mary and then roams the seemingly-unending fair in search of clothes, furniture, supplies, wares and even cattle. This particular feast is famous for cattle and pottery.

Carmona Beach is a true hidden gem along Goa's coastline, offering a tranquil escape from the more crowded tourist hotspots. My recent visit confirmed its reputation as a peaceful paradise, and I was thoroughly impressed with everything it had to offer.
What struck me most was the serene ambiance. Unlike the bustling beaches of North Goa, Carmona exudes a sense of calm and tranquility. The beach isn't overly developed, which adds to its charm. You won't find rows of shacks or loud music here. Instead, you'll discover a more authentic Goan experience, with local fishermen going about their daily routines and a laid-back atmosphere that encourages relaxation.
The surrounding scenery is also breathtaking. Lush greenery frames the beach, adding to its secluded feel. It's a great spot for nature lovers and photographers alike. I particularly enjoyed watching the sunset from Carmona; the vibrant colors painting the sky were simply stunning.
While Carmona might not offer the same vibrant nightlife as other Goan beaches, it more than compensates with its peaceful atmosphere and natural beauty. If you're looking for a quiet escape, a place to reconnect with nature, and a taste of authentic Goan life, Carmona Beach is an absolute must-visit. It's a true hidden gem that deserves to be discovered.

The structure in Chimbel village, on the outskirts of Goa’s Panaji, began to fall into ruin after the 1880s when it was confiscated by the then Portuguese government and converted into an old age home and completely fell apart in 1980 after which it was abandoned completely.
Today all that remains of the once impressive chapel is the façade and ruins of the walls covered in overgrown plants. The land was being eyed by the government for setting up a sewage treatment plant but the villagers had a different idea.
“Right from my childhood, I remember coming with my parents to the Mount Carmel Chapel… We used to light a lot of candles and serve snacks… There was a beautiful big garden with a fountain inside,” a resident of Chimbel, Fernandes recalls.

The villagers came together to reclaim the last green space in their village and develop it into an ‘archaeological park’.
“Chimbel is lacking in many respects. We have lots of issues like garbage, especially on account of the slum colony, we don’t have proper water supply, no proper health centre, no post office, no police station despite the rising crime,” villager Ana Gracias said.

There is no space remaining for anything in Chimbel anymore either for community service or just a conducive place where people can meet. The chapel is living testimony of the Carmelite and of the village. It is something unique and very, very old. It will give an identity to our village,” Fernandes said.
After several rounds of meetings with Fernando Velho, a conservation architect with the Charles Correa Foundation, the villagers drew up plans for restoring the ruins and making it an easily accessible park.

More than being a symbol of the village, the chapel has a peculiar historical significance—it is the first religious order in Goa to admit local people as Catholic priests.

The Europeans considered themselves as superior and Indians as inferior. Whereas this congregation known as the Chimbel Carmelites broke the ice and they began local congregation,” Fr Archie Gonsalves, a Carmelite priest, explained.

For us, it is a very precious place because it is the heritage of the Carmelites. So, we have joined hands with the villagers and conservationists and it has resulted in the safeguarding the place which a year ago would have got completely destroyed and gone into a sewage plant,” Gonsalves said.
For now, the villagers hope to gather the funds and preserve what’s left of a part of their history

A vibrant tapestry of sights, sounds, and smells, Mapusa Market is an absolute must-visit for anyone wanting to experience the authentic buzz of Goa. While Friday is the main market day, the weekend still holds a fantastic charm, offering a kaleidoscope of choices, especially for dresses and fresh produce.
A Shopper's Paradise for Dresses
For fashion enthusiasts, the market is a treasure trove. You'll find a delightful array of dresses, from breezy, colorful beachwear perfect for Goa's tropical climate to more traditional Indian attire. Stalls are laden with vibrant textiles, printed skirts, and trendy tops. Don't be shy to bargain; it's all part of the fun and expected by the friendly vendors. The sheer variety ensures that you'll find something to suit your style and budget. Whether you're looking for a unique souvenir or a complete wardrobe refresh, the dress selection here won't disappoint.
A Feast for the Senses: The Vegetable Market
The vegetable section of the market is a riot of color and life. Local farmers proudly display their fresh, seasonal produce. From plump red tomatoes and leafy green spinach to exotic vegetables and aromatic herbs, the quality is exceptional. The air is filled with the earthy scent of fresh produce and the lively chatter of vendors and customers. It's a fantastic opportunity to sample some of Goa's local flavors and pick up ingredients for a delicious home-cooked meal. Even if you're not planning on cooking, a stroll through this section is a cultural experience in itself.

Mapusa Market is a vibrant and traditional Goan marketplace, best visited on Fridays when it’s packed with local vendors selling everything from farm produce to ethnic crafts. It's the perfect place to experience authentic Goan culture and flavours.

🔑 Highlights:

🥖 Must-try: God Poi – a traditional Goan whole-wheat bread made with palm jaggery. Soft, slightly sweet, and often sold warm at the market. A delicious local treat you shouldn’t miss!

🍖 Other Must-buys: Goan sausages (chorizo), cashews, spices, bebinca (layered dessert), kokum, pickles, and local pottery

🧺 Also Find: Handicrafts, textiles, coconut oil, herbal products, and clay ware

🗓️ Best Time: Friday mornings (8–11 AM)

💵 Pro Tip: Carry cash, wear comfy shoes, and stay alert in crowds

💰 Bargaining: Common and expected

The church, also known as 'The Ponda Church', is an important landmark in the region and is dedicated to the patron saint of mothers and families.

The atmosphere within the temple is one of tranquility and peace, making it an ideal place for introspection and meditation. Visiting the Bhagavathi Temple is not just a spiritual experience, but also an opportunity to immerse oneself in the rich cultural heritage of the region. The temple is a place of great historical and cultural significance, and a visit here offers a glimpse into the traditions and beliefs that have shaped the local community.

Overall, the Bhagavathi Temple is a must-visit destination for anyone seeking a deeper connection with their spirituality and a greater understanding of the cultural heritage of Goa. Its stunning architecture, peaceful atmosphere, and spiritual significance make it a truly special place to visit.

Hindus describes Mahalaxmi is a form of Mother of all Universes, who raised three super powers Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver and Shiva the destroyer.
This temple is built in the hollows of valley; the description of this temple goes this way, it has a small arched entrance at the one end with naubat khana placed on the up and further to this is a village. Two sides are kept open, in a miscellany of separate shrine parivar devatas are place displaying in the courtyard, with a simple plastered covering in a red colour. On the entrance of this main building there is a domed octagonal temple tower place with very rare two domes having the look of flattened which is something attractive, the main towers truncated dome is kept higher with huge lantern.
This floor has new hall designed for dance and musical activities keeping in mind with festivals. Every side of mandapa’s entrance is designed with the arts of Hanuman who is known God of Monkey and Garoda Vishnu’s vehicle, half eagle half man and the doors are magnificently carved in wood placed with Ganesh on them.

A dynamic silver arched doorway which takes you from pillared hall to sanctuary, the best part is the creation of twenty four wooden panels painted lightly, thus displaying the pictures of Bhagvata Puran along with the story of Lord Krishna and Vishnu’s eighth incarnation. The actual main temple of Mahalaxmi is situated in Kolhapur one of Maharashtra’s state which is nearly 150 km away from Goa to the north. 4kms. from Ponda. Situated in the village of Bandode.

It is considered the abode of the original Goddess of the Shakti cult. The Sabhamandap has a gallery of 18 images, out of 24 images of emanatory aspects of Bhagvata sect, which is considered one of the few galleries of wooden images of Vishnu in India . The image of Mahalakshmi has a close resemblance to that of Mahalakshmi at Kolhapur , the main centre of worship. Her special feature is that she wears a linga on her head and is considered a peaceful or Satvik form of the Devi. The Goddess Mahalakshmi was worshipped by the Shilahara rulers (750-1030 A. D.) and the early Kadamba Kings of Goa.

ABOUT SHREE MAHALAXMI TEMPLE
Mahalaxmi is the Goddess of power and strength and is believed to be an incarnation of ‘Adishakti’-the supreme form of power and energy. The Shaktas- worshippers of Shakti cult, among the Saraswats, worshipped Adishakti in the form of the linga.

Wedding Halls:Kalyan Mantap is a wedding hall service offered by the Devasthan than to the devotees. Those who want to start their new beginning or perform any auspicious function near the feet of the Goddess Mahalaxmi can book the hall and perform the rituals.
There are 2 halls
1)Out of two one hall is big and suitable for weddings and other bigger function with an attached buffet hall. One can book this hall with the Devasthan in advance for any bigger function like a wedding.
2)The second hall is a bit smaller as compared to the first one and can be suitable for small religious rituals like poojas, and Devkaryas.

Accommodation:Shree Mahalaxmi Devasthan offers accommodation to the devotees who come from other sates to pay their prayers and devotion to the Goddess Mahalaxmi. Rooms are available at an affordable rate with all the basic amenities for a better experience. Rooms are clean, and furnished with the bed, table, chair, and mirror. Devasthan has two types of rooms AC(Air conditioner) and Non-AC (Without air conditioner). Devotees can choose the rooms as per their requirements and can stay for days. Since rooms are within the premise of the temple, one can visit the temple anytime they wish to and offer prayers.

Parking:Temple has a very larger parking area which can accommodate several cars at a time. The parking area is within the premise of the temple and the temple is at a walkable distance. Cars and bikes parked at the parking area are very much safe and secure.

Canteen:Devasthan also has a canteen  that serves a complete meal to the devotees. You can have a pure veg meal at this canteen.

The 16thcentury Goa saw the reign of Portuguese and faced their terror intending to spread of Christianity. Goans witnessed the forceful acts of conversion, temple demolitions, breaking of idols of temple deities looting temple wealth and setting on fire the temple buildings. It is during this period our pious ancestors put themselves to risk of life. Leaving behind their homes, property, wealth, agricultural land and even their family and the near and dear ones escaped into the moonless nights across the border with the family deities and their symbols. They crossed through the dense forest, valleys, rivers and hills to set up again the more precious than life image of the family deity in a new temple to protect and nurture the Hindu religion for benefit of future generations.
The temple of Shree Shantadurga  Shankhawaleshwari is located in a quiet and serene place, an experience beyond description. Areca groves touching the sky, gurgling sweet water streams and brooks, stretch soothing vistas of green carpeted hillsides, dense bushes and scenes of natural beauty embrace you with pleasant smell of forest flowers.

A flight of steps from the tar road leads to the Mahadwar of the Temple complex. Between the Mahadwar and the main temple of Shree Shantadurga  Shankhawaleshwari  is the deepasthambha and Tulshi Vrindavan in the middle courtyard. The temple faces purva disha with sodiyo that’s the viewers area followed by mahachowk . Recently being renovated the mahachowk  shows contemporary touch in the construction of the pillars, beams and the balcony that runs all three sides except the garbhagriha.

Through the dwar of the garbhagriha you get the glimpse of panchadhatu  idol of Shree Shantadurga Shankhawaleshwari installed on a pedestal . The religious minded devotees are transfixed and dumbstuck by the sheer spectacle and beauty of the goddess.  The devotees get rid of their doubts and fears and experience peace of mind and bow to the supreme power.

In the mantap near the idol are three similar idols of Shree Laxmi Narasinha, Shree Vijayadurga and Lord Ganapati. The mantap is crafted in silver and engraved with fine handiwork. At the floor level just touching the main pedestal is a small panchadhatu idol of goddess which s used for Prasad kowl ceremonies. Behind the main deity is a roinn (Anthill) not visible to those standing at the main door of the garbhagriha. The flooring of garbhagriha, mahachowk, porch, aisle and pradakshina is done with marble and exquisite tiles.

The right of the temple is Agrashala, initial portion for the residence of the priests and archaks. The asthakoni mahachowk and the elevated three spires and two domes structure of the temple give it a beautiful and holy appearance. The temple is lined from behind by eight small temples and garbhagrihas, six of which are installed lingas signifying purvapurushas. The other two include deity of the Grampurusha and Shree Dandapani or Kshetradhipati.

There also appears a tree of ancient origin considerd to be of the devachara where every year gifts are given in form of food like ront to seek blessings. This is where sankhliyo is venerated by the devotees.

Kapileshwar Temple is the first as you start to drive west towards the biggest cluster of six temples. Old ladies, sitting on a small flight of stairs at this entry, selling flowers, incense and coconut to be offered to the deities inside are likely to greet you. A small altar with Tulsi or holy basil adorns the courtyard. While worshiping trees is common in Hinduism, Tulsi is at the top of that totem pole and as such, you are likely to see Tulsi not just in temple courtyards but also inside private homes across the country.

Compared to its peers, this 18th century temple is relative simple. The characteristic red laterite-rock construction of Goa lays bare and adds to its rustic charm. While the mandapa has an elegant gable-style roof, the garbagriha or the sanctum is housed inside a beautiful dome-shaped structure. The other thing you would notice is that this is a relatively quiet temple as compared to others in the area. Mondays are special prayer days for Lord Shiva and expect more people on this day of the week.

Visiting the spice farm is definitely worth it. It's a privately owned farm spread over 130 acres, though only 2–3 acres are accessible to visitors. The guided tour is informative, offering great insights into various spices, their Ayurvedic benefits, and how to identify fake products often sold in the market.

The entry fee is INR 500 per person, which includes a guided tour, farm visit, and lunch. The food was delicious, healthy, and they even offer Jain/Swaminarayan options, making it completely vegetarian-friendly.

Since the farm is located away from North Goa, it's best to go by car for convenience.

Stepping onto this 150-year-old spice plantation owned by the Shetye family(been in generation) felt like a journey back in time, and a welcome escape from the typical tourist trail. Unlike the crowded, bustling tours you find elsewhere, this place offers a truly serene and personal experience. It's clear from the moment you arrive that the hosts are passionate about quality over quantity, carefully curating a peaceful environment for every guest.

The heart of this experience is the host,Vrushali Kelekar, a truly kind, extremely knowledgeable and an engaging conversationalist. Her warm hospitality made us feel less like visitors and more like cherished friends.
The culinary highlight was a divine meal prepared by the host's daughter. Her Gaud Saraswat Brahmin food was not just delicious but tasted like a labor of love, a true reflection of authentic Goan home cooking.

What made the experience even more memorable was the unique feni ritual. We were introduced to the local tradition of sipping feni with perfectly roasted cashews and tor, a combination that elevated the spirit-tasting into a truly cultural event. It's these small, personalized touches that set this plantation apart.

If you're looking for a peaceful, authentic, and genuinely heartfelt encounter with Goan culture, history, and food, this is the place. It is a rare find—an unhurried sanctuary that leaves you feeling rejuvenated and deeply connected to the soul of Goa.

5 stars to MrSachin Shetye for his personal attention and care for his guests at his beautiful heritage. He took us through the plantation and explained everything in detail, all by himself. Loved the artefacts carved out of coconut shells. Must visit place in Goa.

I had the pleasure of visiting Savoi Plantation, and it turned out to be one of the most memorable experiences of my trip. From the moment we arrived, we were welcomed with warm hospitality that instantly made us feel at home. The hosts were incredibly courteous, attentive, and ensured every guest was comfortable throughout the visit.

The guided tour of the plantation was both informative and engaging. Our guide patiently explained the wide variety of spices, fruits, and herbs grown there, detailing their uses not only in cooking but also in traditional medicine. It was fascinating to see how each spice is cultivated and to learn stories behind their significance in Goan culture.

A major highlight of the visit was the authentic Saraswat cuisine served for lunch. The spread was absolutely delightful — freshly prepared, flavorful, and true to the traditional Goan-Saraswat style of cooking. Each dish carried a unique taste, perfectly balanced with local spices straight from the plantation. It was the kind of meal that leaves a lasting impression and makes you want to return just for the food.

The combination of delicious food, heartfelt hospitality, and an enriching plantation tour made this visit special. Savoi Plantation offers not just a glimpse into spice farming, but also an opportunity to experience Goan culture in its most authentic form.

Highly recommend this place for anyone visiting Goa who wishes to enjoy something beyond beaches — a perfect blend of learning, culture, and flavors!

🌿 A Must-Visit Gem in Goa’s Heartland
I recently visited Tanshikar Spice Farm in Netravali, and it was one of the most authentic and enriching experiences I’ve had in Goa. Owned by Mr. Chinmai Tanshikar, whose family has nurtured this land for over 250–300 years, the farm spans 23 lush acres and is a living example of sustainable, organic farming.
From arecanuts, cardamom, coffee, maize, honey, pepper, and countless other spices, everything grown here is 100% organic—and available for purchase directly from the source. The guided tour was both educational and immersive, and the staff were incredibly friendly and always ready to help, making the experience feel personal and warm.
The food is simple, home-cooked, and deeply nourishing, prepared mostly with ingredients sourced from the farm itself or nearby homegrown plots. Meals are lovingly crafted by Mr. Chinmai’s mother and a few professional chefs, blending tradition with care. You can truly feel the freshness in every bite—it leaves you not just satisfied, but glowing from within.
What truly sets this place apart is its eco-conscious spirit. They offer day and night treks, and within the estate flows a serene waterway that leads to a natural pool—perfect for a refreshing dip. Even more inspiring is their commitment to animal rescue, caring for stray dogs, snakes, and birds with compassion and dedication.
This isn’t just a farm, it’s a sanctuary of nature, culture, and kindness. If you're ever in Goa, Tanshikar Spice Farm is a place you must visit at least once in your lifetime.

"A Green Escape in Goa"

Bhagwan Mahavir Wildlife Sanctuary, Goa Overview

Bhagwan Mahavir Sanctuary is a 240 sq km protected natural habitat located in the Western Ghats of India, on the Goa-Karnataka border. Touted to be Goa's largest wildlife reserve, it is home to the famous Dudhsagar Falls, Mollem National Park, Tambdi Surla Temple, and Devil's Canyon among other attractions. It houses a variety of plants, birds, and animals and thus is popular amongst nature lovers and hikers.

The green zone of Bhagwan Mahaveer Wildlife Sanctuary consists of west-coast semi-evergreen, tropical-evergreen and moist deciduous forests that create a natural habitat for a wide variety of animals and birds. It is home to the Dhangar community and has temples built by the Kadamba Dynasty. The park is also home to a community of nomadic buffalo herders known as Dhangar.

The area covered by the sanctuary is heavily forested and is famous for pristine vegetation - West Coast tropical evergreen forests and deciduous forests which are found on the higher altitudes along the banks of perennial rivers. The state bird of Goa, Ruby-throated Yellow Bulbul is the most common of 120 species of birds found here. The primary species of trees found include Terminalia, Xylia and Timber trees. Due to density, sunlight does not reach the forest floor in many places. The trees are home to an estimate of 722 species of flowering plants and 128 species of plants.

Apart from greenery, the sanctuary is the natural habitat of several species of animals including Deer, Sambar, Spotted deer, Hof, Tiger, Panther, Toddy cat, Leopard cat. In addition to these, one can also spot civet, bonnet, jackal, types of squirrels, sloth bear, hyena, Golden Oriole, Emerald Dove, Common Grey Hornbill, Malabar Trogan, Scarlet Minivet, Asian Palm Swift, Jungle Owlet, Forest Wagtail, and many others.

We tried to enter, but **high tide had taken over**. The sea covered the path like a curtain, closing off the past until the next chance.

The beach itself is something else. Wide. Wild. Untouched.

Whether you're spiritual, curious, or just seeking beauty that feels **honest and raw**, this place will leave something with you.

Ashvem Beach is a hidden gem that feels magical, especially in the evenings. On rare days, you get to witness a breathtaking natural phenomenon – the sea slowly recedes, revealing the river as it flows to meet the ocean. I visited Ashwem Beach on a weekday during monsoon, after feeling overwhelmed by the chaos of Baga and Calangute. Within minutes of arriving, I realized this place was different — calmer, cleaner, and with a rhythm all its own. I reached there by 4pm and there was around 10 people in the whole beach. The beach stretches out in a wide, lazy arc, with soft sand underfoot and barely any noise except the waves and wind. There were no vendors calling out, no blaring music, just a few scattered beach chairs, a couple of travelers reading books, and the occasional dog napping in the shade of a palm.

What struck me most was the peace — it almost felt like the kind of place you’d want to come to just to breathe a little deeper. I walked for almost an hour without seeing more than a handful of people. A few wooden beach shacks lined the shore, built with bamboo and coconut leaves, blending into the landscape rather than standing out. I stopped at one called La Plage, which had a beautiful, rustic setup and served unexpectedly good French food. I sat there for a long while, watching the waves and sipping something cool, grateful for the quiet. There are a dozen of resorts near this beach that has the beach as a. great backyard. Even if you don’t stay there, you can walk along and get into the resorts and buy beer or alcohol of your choice and continue strolling. My request is please don’t throw wastes here and there any spoil the place anymore.

Ashwem isn’t flashy or dramatic — there are no wild parties or flashy beach clubs. Instead, it offers a kind of slowness that you begin to crave after a few days in Goa. It’s the kind of place where you’d want to stay a week without doing much: wake up with the sun, walk on the beach barefoot, eat slowly, and let your thoughts catch up with you.

If you’re someone who enjoys the idea of Goa not just as a party destination but as a place to rest and reset, Ashwem might be your perfect corner. It felt safe, unpretentious, and genuinely soothing — like a long exhale after too much noise. I left thinking I’d come back again, but next time, I’d stay longer.

Anjunem village, Sattari Taluka, North Goa, India, on the Costi Nadi (a tributary of the Valvanti River under the Mhadei Basin), near the Sanquelim-Belgaum highway and Chorla Ghat, approximately 44 km from Panaji and 10-12 km from Sanquelim.
Purpose: Primarily irrigation, supporting 2,100 hectares of cultivable command area (CCA) with an ultimate irrigation potential of 4,600 hectares, plus drinking water supply and flood control for Sattari and Bicholim talukas and parts of Bardez. It also supports local ecosystems and aquatic life.
Construction: A medium irrigation project, approved in 1977, completed in 1989. It’s a gravity masonry dam, 176 meters long and 42.8 meters high, with a spillway of 39.48 meters and four radial gates (7.62 x 6.85 meters) to manage a design flood of 487 cumecs.
Capacity: Gross storage capacity is approximately 234.361 million cubic meters (MCM), with effective storage at 227.157 MCM. The reservoir covers 17.18 sq.km in the Western Ghats, receiving about 3,730 mm of annual rainfall.
Features: Includes a pick-up weir 1 km downstream and two canals (left bank: 15.5 km, 1.03 cumec; right bank: 25 km, 1.64 cumec). It supports agriculture, provides drinking water (82 MLD raw water to treatment plants), and has hydroelectric potential, contributing to Goa’s energy needs.
Challenges: Siltation from planning flaws and forest depletion has reduced water-holding capacity, causing water scarcity in summer. No detailed environmental impact studies have been conducted since 1987, and afforestation with unsuitable tree species has worsened soil erosion.
Tourism: Surrounded by lush hills, Vagheri hill, and Morlemgad peak, it’s a scenic spot for picnics, boating, fishing, birdwatching “

Canal Fall in Goa is one of those hidden gems that truly captures the untouched beauty of the region beyond its beaches and nightlife. Tucked amidst lush greenery and serene landscapes, this waterfall offers a peaceful escape for those who love nature, photography, and a bit of adventure. The journey to reach Canal Fall is part of the experience — a short trek through forest trails, the sound of chirping birds, and the occasional rustle of leaves as you get closer to the water.

The falls themselves are not massive, but that’s what makes them special — it’s quiet, calm, and feels almost private. The water is clean and refreshing, perfect for a dip on a warm Goan afternoon. The surrounding rocks and trees provide plenty of natural shade, making it a great spot for picnics or just relaxing with friends.

Unlike the more commercialized waterfalls in Goa, Canal Fall retains its rustic charm. There are no food stalls or crowds, so it’s best to carry your own water and snacks, and leave no litter behind.

If you enjoy offbeat destinations and love exploring Goa’s natural side, Canal Fall is absolutely worth visiting. It’s peaceful, scenic, and a reminder that Goa is much more than just beaches and parties.

Apart from just a lake, there are many more places nearby for the tourists as well as locals to visit like the famous and historic temple of Shree Saptakoteshwar Temple located approximately 6.5 km from the lake. There are many more temples around the Shree Saptakoteshwar temple area. There is even the famous temple of Bicholim Shree Shantadurga Temple. There are many more famous and must visit places nearby like Shree Rudreshwar Temple situated approximately 12.5 km from Mayen Lake. The famous waterfall also lies in the same vicinity.
Speaking about the lake, the Mayem Lake is one the best places to visit and a must place to visit apart from just beaches. If one is tired of just seeing the beaches and the crowd, then one should definitely visit this place. Apart from relaxing, one can also take up adventures here like Bungee Jumping from 55 metres and  Boating. However, to enter the lake, one has to pay an Entry Fee of Rs. 10/- only per person. The Entry Fee for Boating is Rs. 200/- only per person. The Entry Fee for Bungee Jumping is Rs. 4110/- plus GST. Being renovated by Goa Tourism, the Lake is now much more beautiful and modern then before as can be seen in the pictures below with huge parking both inside and outside which can accommodate 50 plus cars bikes approximately. Now the addition of Shops, Cafeteria, Garden, etc. at an affordable price makes it even more fun place to visit then before. The place is clean and well maintained with two Toilets one at the Entrance and the other one near the Lake with Special Toilet for Disabled Person which is definitely a must to have. Since this place has well maintained Garden, it's definitely great for photography. The great way to pass time here with your family or loved ones could be by Boating as well as by Entertainment as there's an Amphitheatre as well. Each individual is provided with a Life Jacket before you could enter the boat. The boats doesn't have motors which means it's manual and the max capacity is 4 or a family of 4. There are different types of boats as some has a car like steering while some have got a handle to steer it. Some have 4 paddles while some have only 2. Either an individual can paddle it or both can paddle it at the same time. This place definitely can be a great place for picnic for locals as well as tourists. If one wants to stay here for some days, then there is an accommodation available just the opposite side of the Lake by Goa Tourism itself. It's reasonable and great place to be in because if the view that one can get. Mayem Lake for me is definitely one of the top places in Goa and on top of my list as this place has peace as well as adventures. Special Thanks to Goa Tourism for making this wonderful place even more wonderful!

​The Shree Devi Lairai Devasthan in Shirgao, Goa, is a highly revered temple dedicated to Goddess Lairai, believed to be an incarnation of Goddess Parvati. She is also considered one of the seven divine sisters of Goa. The temple holds great significance for both Hindus and Catholics in the region, symbolizing a unique religious harmony, as the goddess is regarded as the sister of the Virgin Mary of Mapusa.
The faith in the goddess is expressed through unique rituals and traditions passed down through generations. Inside the sanctum, the goddess is not represented by a traditional idol but by a sacred copper pot, or "kalash", symbolizing her divine presence. Devotees, particularly those known as "dhonds," prepare for months with strict penance and fasting to honor the deity.
​The temple is most famous for its annual Jatra, or festival, held in the early part of May. This event attracts hundreds of thousands of devotees from Goa and neighboring states. The festival's highlight is the spectacular Agnidivya, a fire walking ritual where the dhonds, after performing a frantic dance to the rhythm of drums, walk barefoot across a bed of hot embers.
​This breathtaking display of devotion is a testament to the immense faith of the followers who believe that the righteous will be unharmed by the fire. The jatra concludes in the early hours of the morning, reinforcing a strong sense of community and spiritual identity among the devotees. The Lairai Jatra is a powerful cultural and religious event that draws people from all walks of life.
