Shirgao is the holy place of goddess Lairai devi ( श्री लइराई ), Its very old and famous temple. The annual jatra (festival) associated with this shrine features unusual customs and rituals drawn from the area’s tribal past.
This is one of the more famous and more unusual Jatra (Hindu temple festival) celebrated in Goa.  The Jatra takes place in early part of May, when thousands of devotees of Devi Lairai descend on the small town and religious rituals and poojas dedicated to the Goddess are performed throughout the auspicious day. Hundreds of people from the villages in surrounding areas, also take part in these celebrations.

The Shirgao Jatra takes place in early part of May. The festival begins early in the morning and continues throughout till dawn. The devotees (dhond) take a bath and walk all the way uphill to the temple to worship the Goddess. Late into the night, as midnight approaches, the devotees perform a frantic dance inside the temple, which is all lit up for the occasion. The dance sessions end around midnight. Next a fire is made using a huge pile of wood kept in a large clearing near the temple.
The final and most spectacular part of the jatra then begins. In the early hours of the morning when the fire has died down, the raking of the coals begins. The devotees await their turn to walk on the holy path of hot coals. Around 4 a.m., the actual ritual starts, with the devotees running through the hot coals carrying their sticks with the name of Devi Lairai. It is said that the fire does no harm to the just devotees who walk calmly through the embers. The unjust are said to hurry through running through the burning coals....

The Shantadurga Temple in Assonora, Moitem, Goa is a vibrant and significant place of worship dedicated to the Hindu Goddess Shantadurga. The temple's facade is a striking spectacle of color, adorned with bright orange and red hues. A grand, ornate entrance archway, topped with a distinctive orange dome and multiple flags, welcomes devotees.
​A prominent sign in Devanagari script identifies the temple as "Shri Devi Shantadurga wa Salgan Devalay," indicating its dedication to the goddess. The sign also specifies its location in Asnode, Bardez, Goa. The surrounding area, with its clear blue sky and lush greenery, provides a serene backdrop for the temple's vibrant structure.
​The architecture is characterized by a blend of traditional Hindu temple styles and modern elements. The main entrance features a series of arches and columns decorated with strings of lights and pennants, giving it a festive appearance. The overall design is a reflection of the cultural and religious traditions of the region.
​The temple serves as a central point of religious and cultural activity for the local community. It stands as a testament to the enduring faith and cultural heritage of the area, providing a space for worship and community gatherings.

This temple is notable for being one of the few in India dedicated to Lord Brahma, the creator in the Hindu trinity. The temple houses a beautifully chiseled black stone idol of Brahma, dating back to the 12th century during the Kadamba period. Shri Brahmadev Ji Temple (Brahma Temple) in Brahma Karmali (also Nagargao), Sattari taluka, Goa, is one of the rare temples in India dedicated to Lord Brahma—the creator—making it a unique & significant cultural gem of the region.

---

📜 History & Legend

Origin & Upshift: The temple dates back to the Kadamba period, around the 12th century. The black stone idol is a chaturmukhi (four-faced) sculpture, notable for the bearded front face and rich Kadamba-era artistry  .

Portugues Inquisition Escape: Around 1541, fearing destruction by the Portuguese, devotees spirited the idol from Carambolim in Old Goa (Tiswadi) through dense forests to the then-independent Sattari  .

Place shaping: The reception site, initially “Chandivade”, eventually took the deity’s name—Brahma Karmali—melting the old village name “Karmali” with Lord Brahma’s presence  .

---

🛕 Architecture & Iconography

Temple Layout: Simplicity defines its design—square garbhagriha, mandapa, and plinth for the idol  .

The Idol: Standing ~1.5 m tall on a three-tiered pedestal, carved from black basalt, the central Brahma has a beard, holds a rosary, Vedas, kamandalu (water pot), and fire ladle (sruva), and is flanked by goddesses Saraswati and Gayatri  .

---

🗓 Rituals & Nearby Nature

Daily Pooja is performed by the resident priest, though the sanctum is often secured behind a grill—visible through openings  .

Brahmotsav: Celebrated every December (Margashirsha Tṛtīyā), this festival draws large local crowds  .

Natural surroundings: Nestled in verdant Western Ghats, the temple is near perennial springs, paddy terraces, betel-nut groves, and is adjacent to a sacred stream  .

---

💡 Why Visit?

Historical rarity: Apart from Pushkar (Rajasthan) and one in Khajuraho (M.P.), temples for Lord Brahma are exceedingly rare  .

Art and atmosphere: Its exquisite Kadamba sculpture, tranquil rural setting, and living heritage rituals make it a serene retreat & culturally enriching stop.

Cultural revival: Recently renovated with support from Goa Tourism & local leadership via a ₹1.37 cr beautification project—enhanced pathways, lighting, seating, and entry porticos—for improved pilgrim comfort and aesthetics  .

---

🕰 Visitor Info

Timings: Open daily, 7 AM–9 PM  .

Access: About 6 km north of Valpoi via tribal forests of Sattari. Entry through steps and side portals.

Best time: Visit during Brahmotsav in December or pair with a nature walk through the Mhadei‑region springs and forests.

---

✨ In Summary

Shri Brahmadev Ji Temple at Brahma Karmali is a rare survivor of Brahma worship, preserved through tumultuous times and enshrined with nature and art. It's a must-visit for heritage seekers, spiritual explorers, and anyone intrigued by Goa's non-colonial history.

An ecotourism destination at the intersection of Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka, the lush green Chorla Ghat was once used by thieves to hide from the British. Chorla is derived from the word 'chor', which means thief...

Adorned with waterfalls and exotic species, Chorla Ghat is a perfect representation of the beauty of the Western Ghats. It is located on State Highway 4..

It is also home to the 300-year-old Sada Fort, which is said to have been built by Desai Sardar, a soldier in Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj’s army. The fort was regularly visited by Shivaji’s sons -- Chatrapati Sambhaji Maharaj and Rajaram Maharaj – to keep a vigil on Chorla and surrounding areas...

Some of the species found here are Malabar whistling Thrush, Malabar Grey Hornbill, Indian Pitta, Nilgiri Wood Pigeon, Loten’s sunbird, Crimson backed sunbird, White Cheeked Barbet, and Nilgiri Flycatcher..

We were a bus of 30 people who came from Goa. The waterfall visit was organised by THQ (Travel Head Quarters), a Goan trek group.
After Dodamarg, the road gets windy and narrow. Be careful while driving as there are interstate big buses also plying on this ghat route. There were a few instances where our bus had to back up, slow down or push into the side to allow other buses and big cars to pass.
The ride was very green and you can see the clouds descended. The twin waterfall is at the top of the mountain. It was full of gushing water in July 2025 first week.
There is a parking lot where our bus was parked. On Sunday, the lot quickly filled up with lots of two wheelers and four wheelers.
The waterfall can be reached by just a ten minute hike from the road, very easy to reach, the route is adjacent to the fall catchment area. At any given time around 300 people can be accommodated at the falls but only for a few minutes. Do not attempt to go up through the waterfall route to the catchment area, it is very slippery and unsafe.
Advisable to wear sturdy sandals or footwear with good grip. I have seen old ladies in kashta navari saree & local kids in simple rubber slippers climb up but then they are locals and used to the terrain.
The local villagers are very helpful and regulate the area. The parking attendant collected fees, there were female and male police officers on the scene and there was a crowd of more than a thousand people enjoying the falls and parking lot. The crowds tend to dump garbage and plastic which is an very irresponsible act. There are no toilets or proper changing rooms in the area. Just makeshift tin sheds.
There are a few local family run eating options which served omelette pav, onion & mirchi pakodas, chicken gravy rice, chips, cold drinks, tea, etc at a very nominal price. And recommend to buy from them to keep the local economy going & reduce garbage waste.
Maximum time spent at the area could be two hours.

The backwater, now a placid expanse, mirrors the cerulean sky, kissed by the golden rays of the sun. It is a canvas painted by the hand of divinity, where the water's surface captures the changing moods of the heavens above.

Amidst this picturesque tapestry, a balancing stone stands as a sentinel, a symbol of harmony in the ever-evolving ecosystem. It is a reminder that even the most precarious of elements can find equilibrium in the embrace of nature.

The sky, too, plays host to a friendly habitation, where eagles, nature's own artists, choreograph their aerial ballet. With artistic grace, they dive into the backwater, their sharp talons reaching for the shimmering fish below. It is a spectacle of precision and power, a reminder that in nature's grand theater, every creature plays a vital role in the delicate balance of life.

This transformation, from mire to masterpiece, is a testament to nature's genius, a symphony of life and beauty that stirs the soul and kindles a profound appreciation for the ever-evolving wonders of our world.

The Selaulim Dam, also spelled Salaulim, is a major dam in South Goa, India, located on the Selaulim (or Guleli) River, a tributary of the Zuari River It is a critical component of the Salaulim Irrigation Project, supplying water for both irrigation and drinking to a large portion of the state The dam is situated about 5 km from the town of Sanguem

Key features of the Selaulim Dam include:
*   **Structure** It is a composite earth and masonry dam, standing 42.7 meters (140 feet) high and extending 1,004 meters in length[1][5].
*   **Reservoir** The dam creates the Selaulim Reservoir, which has a water spread area of 24 square kilometers and a gross storage capacity of 234.361 million cubic meters
*   **Spillway** It features a unique ungated "duckbill" or "Morning Glory" type spillway This funnel-like structure allows excess water to overflow, creating a spectacular sight, especially during the monsoon season
*   **Water Distribution** The project was designed to provide irrigation and drinking water. It supplies about 380 million liters per day (MLD) for domestic and industrial use in South Goa and was intended to irrigate over 14,000 hectares of land  It is the primary source of potable water for approximately 55% of Goa's population

### Construction and History
Construction on the Selaulim Dam began in 1976 and was completed in 2000[1]. The project led to the submergence of 20 villages, displacing around 3,000 people who were subsequently resettled. Several historical and archaeological sites were also relocated, including a 5th-century BC Mother Goddess figure and a 10th–11th century temple, which were carefully dismantled and reassembled at new locations

### Tourism and Local Impact
The Selaulim Dam is a popular tourist destination, particularly during the monsoon season when the reservoir overflows The site features well-maintained gardens, and the surrounding area offers serene, scenic view The dam is open to visitors from 9 am to 6 pm, with a small entry fee

After spending about six days in North and South Goa by the beach, our two nights at Nature’s Nest felt like a complete change of scene — peaceful, green, and deeply refreshing. The drive to the resort was lined with thick greenery on both sides, and once we entered the property, it truly felt like being in the middle of a jungle — just green everywhere.

The rooms were clean, well-kept, and spacious, with a double bed, an extra cot, and a small veranda in front. The food was outstanding. They served authentic Goan cuisine for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, and across both days there was constant variety — no repetition at all. Every meal brought something new and delicious, and the team took great care to make sure we were happy and comfortable with our food.

The nature activities organized by the resort were exceptional. We went on guided walks where the team explained local spices, birds, insects, and their habitats. The night jeep safari was another highlight — they put in real effort to spot animals by torchlight and identify them from the reflection in their eyes.

The people running the place — Prasad, Raghu, Bhakti, and others whose names I might not recall — were all extraordinary. Passionate about nature and full of knowledge, they made the experience so much richer with their explanations and warmth.

Overall, I would highly, highly recommend Nature’s Nest. It’s an exceptional experience and a must-visit whenever you’re in Goa.

Anshi National Park, located in the Western Ghats of Karnataka, is a peaceful and green paradise for nature lovers. The park is well known for its dense evergreen forests, rich biodiversity, and serene environment. The roads leading to the park are surrounded by beautiful hills and valleys, giving travelers a refreshing experience.

Inside the park, visitors can find a wide variety of flora and fauna including tigers, elephants, bison, leopards, deer, and several species of snakes and reptiles. It is also a heaven for bird watchers with many rare and colorful birds like hornbills, kingfishers, and eagles. The place is less crowded compared to other parks, which makes it even more enjoyable for those who love quiet natural surroundings.

The park has streams, waterfalls, and thick forest trails that make it ideal for trekking, photography, and adventure activities. The best time to visit is from October to May, when the weather is pleasant. Entry timings are usually in the morning and evening, and an affordable entry fee is charged for visitors.

Overall, Anshi National Park offers a truly wild and natural experience, away from city life, and is a must-visit for wildlife enthusiasts and nature seekers.

We had a memorable and refreshing stay at Dudhsagar Plantation with friends during the monsoon, and it’s safe to say it’s a paradise for nature lovers.

The property is beautifully set amidst lush greenery, with a serene nature trail and even a private waterfall inside the plantation—truly rare and special experiences. One of the absolute highlights was taking a dip in the naturally filtered swimming pool during the rain—a magical, rejuvenating experience that we won’t forget.

The open-to-sky bathrooms added a rustic charm and connection to nature, while the basic but clean rooms ensured comfort. Expect to come across a few bugs and ants—it’s part of the charm when you’re staying deep inside a plantation filled with towering jackfruit trees and dense foliage.

The hospitality was warm—Mr. Ashok was very helpful and informative, always available for any guidance. The restaurant area is well-maintained, offering simple but tasty homemade food. The bar was a surprise treat, stocked with their own fenny and urak—and a special mention to Shivam, who mixed up some really good cocktails!

We also had the company of a few resident dogs. Chocy, though a bit temperamental and best admired from a distance, accompanied us almost everywhere like a quiet guardian. The other dogs on the property were quite friendly and added to the homely atmosphere.

Do note, you’ll need a torch at night to find your way, which only adds to the feeling of being completely immersed in nature.

Overall, Dudhsagar Plantation is ideal if you’re looking to unwind, disconnect, and soak in the monsoon magic of Goa in a truly natural setting. Highly recommended for groups of friends or couples who appreciate rustic charm and nature-centric stays.

If you’re planning a trip to Goa and want to avoid the usual crowds, Patnem Beach is the perfect destination. Unlike the busier beaches of North Goa, Patnem offers a calm, serene, and almost private atmosphere—making it ideal for those who value peace and quiet.

The golden sands and clean waters create a relaxing vibe, and the beach feels less commercialized, which adds to its charm. Kayaking here is an absolute delight and a must-try activity—the calm waves make it safe and enjoyable even for beginners.

This beach is especially recommended for couples who want to spend quality time together without the usual hustle and bustle. Staying at a resort or homestay nearby allows you to enjoy long, peaceful walks on the shore, quiet sunsets, and undisturbed relaxation.

If you want to experience the calmer, more soulful side of Goa, away from the party chaos, Patnem Beach is where you should be.

Patnem Beach is a hidden gem in South Goa. The beach is clean, less crowded, and offers a peaceful environment. The water is clear, making it perfect for swimming.
